sentences.text: Falcarius is the most basal known definitive therizinosaurian genus and is considered a transitional form between typical theropods and the more derived Therizinosauridae.

Although it likely does not belong to Therizinosauridae, the animal is part of the broader group Therizinosauria, which is characterized by wider hips, a large braincase, and long necks typical of plant-eaters.
This dinosaur shared derived traits with therizinosaurids, including a long neck, a small head with plant-eating teeth, a robust arm with large claws, and a vertical body posture.
The name Falcarius means "sickle cutter" in Latin, referring to the animal's large hand claws.
Falcarius possessed a small, elongated skull and a very long neck supported by elongated cervical vertebrae.

The animal retained a relatively long tail, had forelimbs that were not particularly long but showed signs of increasing robustness, and the exceptionally thick epicondyles of the humerus indicate that Falcarius had strong arm musculature.
Falcarius had three toes on its foot that bore weight.
It is assumed that Falcarius was covered in quill-like feathers, similar to less basal Asian therizinosaur specimens.
The smallest Falcarius specimens were under 1 meter long, while average adults reached 4 to 5 meters in length and weighed about 100 kilograms.
Falcarius could reach approximately 1.5 meters off the ground with its long neck to eat leaves or fruit.

Falcarius was a primitive therizinosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically during the Berriasian to Valanginian stages, between 143.1 and 132.6 million years ago.
Falcarius remains were first discovered in 1999 by collector Lawrence Walker at the Crystal Geyser Quarry in Grand County.
More findings occurred in the 2000s, including a second site known as Suarez Quarry reported in 2008 that contained mainly adult individuals of a perhaps slightly different type.

By 2010, the number of Falcarius specimens from the original quarry had risen to over 2,700, and later that year exceeded three thousand, as two extensive bone beds were discovered containing the remains of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Falcarius individuals.

The genus Falcarius contains two species, with the type species Falcarius utahensis formally named in 2005 when a paper was published in the May 2005 issue of the journal Nature by Kirkland and colleagues.
The holotype specimen of Falcarius, UMNH VP 15000, consists of a partial braincase, with many paratypes assigned.
Falcarius had at least sixteen teeth in its upper jaw and twenty-eight teeth in its lower jaw, and it consumed plant material, as indicated by its small, leaf-shaped, and finely serrated upper teeth.
The five longest, straighter, and more pointed teeth in the lower jaw suggest Falcarius might have had a partially omnivorous diet including small animals like lizards.
Falcarius resembles dinosaurs belonging to the Therizinosauridae, a subgroup within Maniraptora.

The species Falcarius suarezarum was originally placed in the distinct genus Geminiraptor in 2010 after Geminiraptor suarezarum was described as a new troodontid species based on an isolated maxilla (specimen CEUM 7319) from the Cedar Mountain Formation. It is debated whether this species belongs to the troodontid genus Geminiraptor or to the therizinosaur genus Falcarius, as initial identification was based on a single jaw bone before later research suggested it was a therizinosaur similar to F. utahensis. A 2026 study by Freimuth, Lively, and Zanno reinterpreted the species "Geminiraptor" suarezarum as a member of Therizinosauria belonging to the genus Falcarius.
